utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-9 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I doubt that they would confuse terms in that way. A military council or military command is one and the same institution. There weren't two such institutions dealing with those matters in the detachment.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know, Your Honour, whether it is the appropriate time for the break. I will be coming back to this document after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take a break and come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have, once again, the last page of the Bosnian version of this document on the screen, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me now quote a sentence from this document. We stopped when we were talking about doubts that the detachment was being controlled by the Bosnian army. It is stated that: "Therefore, the detachment did carry out orders of the army without any right to response. It would carry out these operations and the Allah knows best." Have you found this passage? I wish to ask you the following: How can you explain this right to response?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise to the witness. I'm quoting a part of the document. In the transcript, we have quote the opposite from what I'm saying. Let me repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I said that it says in the document, that the detachment carried out the army's orders without having the right of reply --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that's not what the document says. The document says: "Therefore, had the detachment carried out the army's orders without having the right to reply, then it would have carried out these operations, and Allah knows best." You got to put the word "had" at the beginning of the sentence; otherwise, you're giving it a completely different meaning.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in any event, I'm reading from the Bosnian version. The text was translated from Arabic into Bosnian, and then from Bosnian into English. In any event, the witness has this part of the document in front of him, and I will ask the witness -- I don't know how the translating service did this. I must apologise. I hope you're aware of the situation, that we waited for the translations until the very last moment, and that, so as not to delay this testimony, I was not unable to compare the Bosnian and the English versions. But I will ask the witness to read out this part of the document and to explain it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please explain what -- what is said in the document actually means? Could you read out the Bosnian version and tell us how you understand it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my assistant is telling me that the problem is in the interpretation, that what I am say something being misinterpreted, for your information.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you, Witness, read out and tell us how you understand this part of the document? What is your understanding of this part of the document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-9 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is quite clear to me. This cannot mean anything else but that the detachment was not under the control of the army because, had it been, it would have to carry out all orders regarding combat activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What is stated here in this document, does it reflect the reality with respect to control over the El Mujahedin Detachment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-9 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It does reflect the gist of the relationship with the corps command, the army command; and I think that I spoke about that already in my previous testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I also wish to remind you that, on page 5703 of the transcript of the 16th of November, 2007, I put it to you with regard to the orders coming from the 3rd Corps and the orders whereby the 3rd Corps tried to include the detachment within the corps structure. I suggested it to you that these were just papers, pieces of paper, and that the detachment never accepted such orders, nor to resubordinate. Your answer was: "That is correct." In connection with this document, I wish to ask you: This letter, which is said to be signed and certified by the detachment command, would you agree that it reflects these very facts that you testified about, that the detachment, in fact, would not accept nor carry out orders of the army units in Bosnia and Herzegovina, or rather, of the corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you understood me correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What difference is there between the Shura --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Shura --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could we redact page 58, lines 18 to 25, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to the witness for this mistake. In terms of competencies, what difference is there, in relation to the activities of the detachment, between the Sharia and the military council?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Judge. Before the witness answers, we've got a problem in the English translation. There are two people translating at the same time. Okay. You may answer the question, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Shura is the supreme control body of the El Mujahedin Detachment. The Shura elected the emir of the detachment, determined the policy and strategy of the detachment. The military council or the military command dealt exclusively with military matters; that is, planning and execution of military operations, preparation for military operations, concerning itself with military logistics, training, and the like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another small question still in connection with this document and relating to the fact that the detachment was entitled to respond. Does this mean that it also had the right to refuse to obey the orders, or did this mean that they confronted their superiors when such orders were given?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The El Mujahedin Detachment, on a number of occasions, refused to take part in operations that were required of it by the superior command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, document D 1109 will become Exhibit number 1394.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: While testifying, you answered many questions relating to logistics in the detachment. On 15 November 2007, on page 5644 of the transcript, you said: "Throughout the time I was in the detachment, the detachment resolved logistic matters on its own, purchasing resources. It did not have the assistance of the army, nor was it issued by the army." Will you please look at a document, 1201. It's a lengthy exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like the witness to have a look at this exhibit once again, and I wish the witness to see page 9 of the English version and attachment D001-1289 of the Bosnian version. So page 9 of the English version; and D001-1289 of the Bosnian version. For the record, this is a message sent on the 27th of February, 1995 to the Sheik, His Excellency Anwar Saban.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, this is a short document. Will you please read it, and then I will put my question to you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-9 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to ask you the following, where the document says that: "We have opened an office of the battalion in Kuwait, which is based in my house. Thanks be to God, we have collected around 18.000 DM in just one day. We will send you monthly aid for the battalion. We will also publish news from Bosnia and from the battalion that you will send us by fax," and a signature is Abu Othman Al Kuwait. My question is: Have you heard of this person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-9 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know him personally, Abu Othman Al Kuwaiti, and his name figures on the previous document that you showed us with a list of some 15 names.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Judging by the document, the detachment seemed to have had an office in Kuwait, which collected monthly funds. Is that true, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-9 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know that Abu Othman was the connection with Kuwait, and he collect the funds there for the El Mujahedin Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this document is already an exhibit so we can remove it, and I have no further questions for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-9 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Welcome back to the Tribunal. Before we start, I have just a couple of preliminary type of questions for you. Since the time, sir, that you left the Tribunal last November until coming back here presumably yesterday or the day before, did you have any contact with any members of the Office of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-9 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, during that same time-period from when you left last November until returning in mid-April, did you have any contact with any members of the Defence team in this case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-9 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you perhaps explain what you mean by this contact or your last answer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-9 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had contact with Mr. Remzija Siljak. I believe that he is an investigator for the Defence. He asked me if I could help them to get in touch with a witness who might testify about the reports that were sent from the detachment abroad, to the countries abroad. I had said to him that Abu el Masri would have been the best witness who was the personal secretary of Sheik Enver; however, he could not be reached because he was in Egypt and not Bosnia. That was the extent of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately when you had this discussion with Mr. Siljak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-9 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some 15 to 20 days ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And at that point in time, sir, did Mr. Siljak or anyone else show you the documents that you have looked at this morning in court?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-9 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only saw one of the documents, one of these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you remember which one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-9 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I don't know the number that it bears now, but the one entitled, "My dear Sheik," and which speaks of some problems listed in ten points.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And other than this document then, sir, that's the only document Mr. Siljak showed to you, some 15 to 20 days ago?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-9 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the only document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And where were you, sir, when you were shown this document by Mr. Siljak some 15 to 20 days ago?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-9 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We met in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And can you recall, sir, approximately how long you were with Mr. Siljak on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-9 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me return to a general topic that was discussed earlier today in your testimony. You mentioned earlier - and I believe this is it on page 18 of the transcript - at the first time when you were shown some of these documents that were sent abroad, you identified these documents as being the bulletins of the El Mujahedin Detachment. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-9 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And I believe, if I'm not mistaken, you told us that this bulletin, the title of this document or documents was: "Call to Jihad"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-9 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Bosnian, "Zov Dzihada."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which means, Interpreter?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "The Call of the Jihad."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, this bulletin, Call to Jihad or Call to the Jihad, can you tell us, was this a regularly published bulletin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-9 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a regular report sent abroad. Later on, it was planned to be published as a magazine in the Bosnian language. I think that one issue of the magazine was even published toward the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And this Call to Jihad bulletin or magazine, how frequently was it compiled and put together and distributed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-9 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately - I don't know for a fact, as Abu Haris was in charge of that, as well as some other members of the press centre of the detachment - I believe that the bulletin was made once monthly, with the exception of the situation when the detachment was engaged in operations and when there were intense combat activities ongoing. In such situations, some of the centres received the bulletins on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, in response to that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm a bit confused by that answer. We are told that this bulletin was a monthly bulletin; and in situations when there was activities, combat activities, it was done on a daily basis. Is that what you said, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not a bulletin as such, reports were sent almost daily to centres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, in response to my last question, you said Abu Haris was in charge of that, as well as some other members of the press centre of the detachment. These bulletins, or this Call to the Jihad publication, what role did the press centre of the detachment play with respect to the production of these publications?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-9 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you clarify your question? I'm not sure I understand it fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, I asked you how frequently the Jihad bulletin or magazine was published. And on page 64, lines 17 through 19, you answered: "Approximately - I don't know for a fact, as Abu Haris was in charge of that as well as some other members of the press centre of the detachment - ..." And my question is: What role the press centre of the detachment played in producing the Call to the Jihad bulletin or magazine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-9 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a sort of editorial board, and we could say that Abu Haris was its editor in chief. There was Nedim Haracic, and Muris Lubancic even worked in the office for a while. They gathered information, produced reports, and then those that were compiled in the Bosnian would be translated into Arabic and sent abroad.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So I take it then, sir, from your answer, that these Arabic language bulletins or reports that we've seen today were produced by the press centre, in terms of a public relations aspect, to be sent abroad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-9 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, why - and I know you have touched on this a little, but I would like to you elaborate on that - can you tell us why it was important for the detachment to produce these bulletins, this Call to the Jihad, and to send those outside of Bosnia and Herzegovina during the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-9 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was important that the reports be sent because the friends of the detachment who were supporting the detachment wanted to be kept abreast of what was going on in the detachment. I think it is only a natural thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And when you say, sir, "the friends of the detachment who were supporting the detachment," that would include funding sources?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-9 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Primarily, the funding sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, if this Call to the Jihad bulletin had any effect in terms of recruiting for the detachment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-9 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Presumably. I can't be certain about it. The recipients of the reports from the detachment passed the information on, and conducted some sort of propaganda, as it were, for the detachment. Quite a few individuals joined the detachment. Whether that was the result of among other things the bulletin, too, I cannot state that with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, when you say "the recipients of the reports from the detachment passed the information on and conducted some sort of propaganda, as it were, for the detachment," what do you mean by that? How was that information passed on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-9 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me give you an illustration which will give you a clear idea of how this worked. For instance, in Saudi Arabia, there was Abu Mauz who was in charge of raising funds and who received the reports from the El Mujahedin Detachment. He used that information to visit Sheiks ànd rich men, potential donors. He also brought along the video recordings that we made in the detachment. It was also distributed; and as a result of that, donations and funds flowed in. That was the immediate result.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, if the information that was passed on from the Call to Jihad bulletin or publication was spread by way of word of mouth in mosques outside of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-9 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us, these funds that were being received from outside, what was being done with this money or these funds?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-9 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The funds were used for purchasing ammunition, weapons, food, clothes, equipment, whatever the El Mujahedin Detachment needed, communications devices, vehicles, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I take it from your answer that all of these items that you have listed were being used in order to advance the war aims.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-9 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Largely, to a great extent. There were some humanitarian activities, too; but for the most part, the purpose was to advance the war aims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I take, sir, from your previous answer with respect to the document that was shown to you that expressed a number of doubts, that it was important for the outside funding sources to know that the detachment did not consider itself part of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, objection. Mr. Mundis has forgotten that he is not in the position to cross-examine the witness. This is it his witness, and this is re-examination and not cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'll perhaps move on from that subject and maybe return to it later. I will withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, during the course of the period in time when you were a member of the El Mujahedin Detachment, do you know how many issues or bulletins or Call to the Jihad were sent abroad during that time-period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-9 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't talk in terms of numbers. I don't know exactly. I told you roughly that the bulletin was issued once monthly, and that reports were sent out more often at the time when the detachment was engaged in operations. Throughout my time as a member of the detachment, the -- this was not the case because this was the practice that was introduced in mid-1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd ask that the witness be shown the document marked 65 ter P02025.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before that, let us clarify one matter. My understanding was that the Trial Chamber restricted the cross-examination to the new documents and the so-called Italian collection only. It was not my understanding that we would be going back to the documents that were either shown to the witness or could have been shown to the witness, because they were in the possession of the OTP earlier on. Let me state this in advance. I will be opposing the attempt to go beyond the scope of the cross-examination, since I understood it that my cross-examination was to be restricted to the new documents only. I believe that this should apply to the Prosecutor, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, before I respond, I would respectfully that the witness be escorted out of the courtroom, so as not to potentially prejudice anything that might happen from this point forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please be excused for some moments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. Something is said that is mentioned on the transcript that I said, and I don't remember ever saying this, "motor vehicle accident," at page 69, line 15. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution certainly did not interpret the Trial Chamber decision allowing the Defence to recall the witness to be limited exclusively to newly disclosed material. I don't, with all due respect to my learned colleagues from the Defence, I don't think that is actually the issue here. The issue that has been presented by the further cross-examination of this witness goes to the broader issue of these bulletins and their transmission outside of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina for purposes which my learned colleagues I'm sure, will be arguing vigorously during closing arguments in this case. It is the Prosecution position that, having opened the door and shown the witness a number of these bulletins, that the Prosecution should be allowed to show these bulletins or some of these similar bulletin-type documents to the witness, so that the Trial Chamber has a broader understanding of some of the information that was contained in these bulletins that went outside of Bosnia and Herzegovina. These are not -- the ones we're proposing to show, I will put very clear on the record, are not newly discovered or newly disclosed material. They were on the Prosecution original 65 ter list. But it is it our position that, having opened the door to this issue, the Prosecution is entitled to put similar documents, and we have five of them on the exhibit list disclosed to the witness before witness appeared this morning. We have five such documents on the original 65 ter list that we are proposing to show to the witness for the simple reason that the Defence have now opened the door to this issue, and we believe it is important for the Chamber to have a broader view as to what's contained in these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, can I ask that when your learned friend is responding to what you said to keep seated until he has finished; then when he sits down, I will call you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That's actually all, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood my colleague Mr. Mundis to have finished his submission. Your Honour, the practice, the case law when it comes to re-examination before this Tribunal has been established beyond any doubt. In all of the cases I am aware of before this Tribunal - and I am referring to the Oric case primarily - all the cases allowed additional cross-examination in such situations as involve a party to the proceeding that did not have occasion to present some documents to a witness. Now, today the Prosecutor claims, without any compunction in relation to the entire case before us and in relation to the prejudice plead to the Defence with their actions, claims that the Defence has opened the door to these questions to be put by the Prosecutor through the very fact that the Defence showed these documents to the witness. Your Honours, this is a terrible, terrible, terrible omission on the part of the Prosecutor who kept some documents in a drawer for three years. Not only did they keep these documents in their drawer, they had the obligation to show the documents to the witness when he testified earlier on, and I'm referring to the documents that I showed the witness today. All these documents that are listed here could have been shown to the witness by the Prosecutor. The Prosecutor did not do that. Therefore, it is not the Defence who opened the door to that line of questioning; rather, the Defence was brought into such a position that it had to put these questions only today. It was through the fault of the Prosecution that we came into the situation where I had to show the witness these documents because the Prosecutor did not show them; and, therefore, this cannot be the basis for his argument that I opened any doors. Your Honours, I appeal to you to honour the case law of the Tribunal and to restrict the examination to the documents that I use in my cross-examination only. The Prosecutor definitely had an opportunity to show both these -- this set of documents and the other documents to the witness earlier on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it possible for the Chamber to be shown the order that re-called the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, the order does not restrict the re-examination. It says that the motion is granted. It allows the Defence to recall Witness PW-9 for the purpose of further cross-examination on the 17th and 18th of April, 2008 and the Prosecution to re-examine the witness on matters arising out of the Defence's further cross-examination. Instruct the Registry's Victim and Witness Section to arrange the appearance of Witness PW-9 before the Trial Chamber on those dates. Prohibits the Prosecution and the Defence to communicate with the Witness PW-9 before his testimony. That's what the order says. Your objection would then perhaps be -- well, I know that you have asked this Court to follow the jurisprudence of the Tribunal, but you have referred us to only the Oric case as the one that you say has dealt with this matter. I'm not quite sure whether you are saying we should follow the Oric case. The Chamber is, however, mindful, of the the appeal, the decision on the interloctory appeal that was filed by the Defence a couple of days ago, and maybe we can take guidance from that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may say the following briefly before that. Your Honour, from the introduction to this document, which refers to the Defence submissions, it is quite clear that we asked for additional examination regarding facts from the new documents, and that is why we were granted this. The Chamber rendered a decision along those lines, Your Honour, because certainly I could have asked this witness many other things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, the document that you were about to show the witness, P02025, is it one of the documents that have just recently come up, or is it a document that you have always had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No. As I said before, Mr. President, it is a document that was originally on the Prosecution 65 ter list. It's always been on there. The issue here, as I also said earlier, in our respectful submission, does not relate to the matter of the late disclosure or the exculpatory material that was disclosed at a later point in time. The issue simple is may I conduct further examination on an issue that arose in the course of the cross-examination. The issue in the cross-examination extensively a number of documents and issues put to the witness concerning documents in the Arabic language that you were sent outside of the Bosnia and Herzegovina. It's that issue, and the contents of information that was being sent outside Bosnia and Herzegovina that I would like to re-examine the witness on. So, in our respectful view, it is a simple matter that is clearly within the discretion of the Trial Chamber. The issue goes to whether we, the Prosecution, can put questions to the witness that relates to the types of documents that were sent outside of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the contents of the information in those documents that was being sent outside Bosnia and Herzegovina. That has been a large focus of the Defence cross-examination showing Arabic language documents that were sent outside of Bosnia. I have five additional documents that were sent outside of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I'd like to put those to the witness and see if those are the same types of documents he was talking about earlier. That is the entire issue here, is whether I can re-examine on issue that's arose in the further cross-examination of this witness and which were manifested through the documents that the Defence showed to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think the order is quite clear on that last point, that the Prosecution to re-examine the witness on matters arising out of the Defence matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the main issue here is to know what prejudice that could occasion to the Defence if the Trial Chamber were to allow the use of a document which, in the words of the Prosecutor, is of the same nature as the documents submitted to the witness during cross-examination today. Could I have an opinion from the Defence on this point?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is it true that these were documents that were on the 65 ter list, but it is it also true that on that list there were several thousand documents which you will appreciate. This type of document, in particular, where the original is in Arabic, and we received this morning information - I think it was this morning - that we were informed that these documents would be used. It will certainly be prejudicial because the Defence did not expect other documents to be discussed here, other than those that were in the new collection. Had we known that, we would have prepared ourselves. We would have checked many things relating to those documents, and we certainly would have had a chance to ask more detailed questions of the witness, because many aspects of these documents arise which we haven't reviewed. We were not able to review them since the moment we were informed that they would be used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just an observation. Your argument is slightly different. You're talking about information, about the late information, the late disclosure. It's not the first argument you put forward before.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was answering your question regarding the prejudice that may fall upon the Defence. I didn't have in mind my previous arguments. In any event, I abide by the initial argument I gave, because I believe that the Prosecutor should have remained within the framework of documents which, due to his error, were not used earlier on. Those he wishes to use today, he could have used with the witness during his previous testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If I may, because there may be some slight confusion, at least based on what I heard Madam Vidovic say in the English language. The issue concerning the five documents that are on the list that were provided to the Defence this morning at 7.47, there is no issue concerning late disclosure of these documents. They were on the 65 ter list. The Defence have had these documents for at least 18 months, if not longer. So it is not an issue of late disclosure of this material. I really regret a situation where arguments are framed in terms of the Prosecution could have done this or the Prosecution could have done that. Similar arguments could be levelled from this side of the courtroom the other direction. I'm not going to do that. I think, as I have said before, the issue is very clear. The issue goes to whether I can cross-examine the witness on the matters arising from the re-examination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sorry. Re-examination the witness on the issues arising from the further cross-examination. If it is an issue that fairness dictates that Madam Vidovic should be allowed to put further questions after I conduct further -- or further examination, re-examination, so it be. We have all day tomorrow for additional questions to be put to the witness concerning the five documents I'm proposing to show to him. So there's not an issue here with respect to prejudice of the accused. They've had these documents for months and months and months and months and months, and that is not the issue. The issue goes to what we can further examine the witness on based upon the further cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I still have a little observation to make as to what the Prosecutor said. It is not just a question or issue of your right to re-examine the witness on issues arising from cross-examination by Ms. Vidovic. That's clear. Of course, you can do that. But it is the question as to whether you can use new documents; that is to say, indeed, documents that were already in your 65 ter list. The question which is here, the contentious one, is whether the documents can be used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought Madam Vidovic is addressing herself to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Judge Lattanzi, you mean, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What did I say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Judge Lattanzi.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, very briefly. What is contentious is precisely what Her Honour Judge Lattanzi said. That is what is contentious. Of course, the Prosecution has the right to examine, but what is in dispute is the use of these particular documents, which the Prosecution had in its possession and which they could have shown the witness when he first testified. That's the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I want to ask Mr. Mundis a question. Mr. Mundis, for what purpose do you want to show the witness these documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would be putting these documents forward for the fact that they go to certain issues that are in dispute, so they would be going in perhaps for the truth of the matter and/or as they relate to the issue of notice. I see that that might be the source of some confusion, and I can explain that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I didn't think it was part of this, and I'm trying to stretch my mind without asking you to show your hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, some, some - I don't believe I'm in a position to state all by any stretch of the imagination - some of these documents that were being faxed by the El Mujahedin Detachment were electronically intercepted by authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina. That's the Prosecution position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see you are standing up, Madam Vidovic. Your colleague is still on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I was just waiting to see if there any further questions. Perhaps, if I could answer the question that Judge Lattanzi, I believe, was putting towards me a few moments ago. Again, with all due respect, I will interpret, when Judge Lattanzi say it is is a question as to whether can you use new documents, I'm interpreting "new" as being material that hasn't been used before in this case and not "new" in the sense of anything that has been late disclosure or anything in that category. With respect to that, Your Honours, the issue here really goes back to a very basic one. The Rules of Procedure and Evidence before this Tribunal allow the cross-examining party to put their case to a witness during cross-examination. Sometimes, as a result of that, the cross-examination goes beyond the scope of the direct examination. In those types of situations, clearly you could imagine a case where the party in re-examination comes back with new or additional documents that weren't shown to the witness during the original direct examination. This issue is exactly the same. If we take away the issue concerning the late disclosure, and in a hypothetical situation let's just assume it was a regular examination, cross-examination, re-examination, because to be quite frank that's exactly what we're talking about: The re-cross and re-examination are the result of the late disclosure, but that is not the issue, in our respectful view. If in a regular or routine direct examination and cross-examination, the cross-examining parties brings up issues outside of the direct, but which relate directly to their case and which the rules specifically allow. In re-examination, the party conducting the re-examination would be allowed to come in with new documents or new material that wasn't on the original exhibit list for that witness, because that's in response to the issues that came up on the cross. It is the same here. It's the same here. The Defence have raised the issue of outside reporting, if you will, transmission of Arabic documents outside of Bosnia and Herzegovina during the course of the cross-examination. They've made that a live issue through this witness. And as a result of that, our view is that the Trial Chamber should be entitled to see evidence of other similar documents that fall into the same category, that relate to the same issue; that is, Arabic large documents that were being sent by the detachment outside of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That's the issue, in our respectful view.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, I do apologise, but I think it is important for you to hear this argument. Mr. Mundis is, very skillfully, trying to tell us that his questions will be within the framework of the cross-examination. However, it is quite clear, from what he has just said, that we were referring to a new category of documents, reports and bulletins which was dispatched abroad. But now Mr. Mundis said that: "The purpose of using these five documents or some of those documents, which I wish to use today, is the question of information, the information which the army had." That did not emerge from my cross-examination. That is quite another legal issue from the one that I have raised here and discussed the factual aspects of that issue. So never for a moment did we go into the question of information that the army may have had; but, rather, we were talking about reports being send to another entity abroad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think the Chamber would like to give a ruling. Madam Vidovic, the Chamber is going to admit those documents and is going to allow the Defence an opportunity to go through those documents that were received this morning, and further examine this witness at a time when the Defence is ready to do so. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, you may proceed Mr. Mundis. P02025.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I don't know if you want me to continue with the witness or if you want to break for the day at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I would have to liked to finish this witness by the end of the day tomorrow. If you are saying break now and forfeit the ten minutes that are remaining --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I will forfeit those ten minutes, Your Honour, in the sense of bringing the witness back in and resuming. I am not even sure I could get through the first anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's call the witness in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If I could, while the witness is being brought in, there was one other just very minor housekeeping issue that I can deal with while the witness is coming in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Earlier this week, the Defence filed a motion seeking to withdraw the 92 bis statement of a witness of whose name I will not mention. The Prosecution is not intending to file any kind of response to that motion, so that issue is ripe for the Trial Chamber's decision and determination. We take no position on any of the issues set forth in that motion at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: For purposes of the witness's entry, may we move into private session.
